1: [Mundaka I 1:1-3 — The higher and the lower knowledge]

Brahmavidya, the knowledge of Brahman, is the foundation of all knowledge. What is that by knowing which all this becomes known? Saunaka, the great householder, approached Angiras and asked this — and the sage answered: There are two knowledges to be known, as the knowers of Brahman have declared: the higher and the lower.

The lower knowledge is the Rig Veda, the Yajur Veda, the Sama Veda, the Atharva Veda, and all their limbs — pronunciation, ritual, grammar, etymology, metre, and astronomy. But the higher knowledge is that by which the Imperishable is apprehended — that which is invisible, ungraspable, without family, without caste, without sight or hearing, without hands or feet.

As the spider sends forth and draws in its thread, as plants grow on the earth, as hair grows on the head and body of a living person — so from the Imperishable arises all that is here. And as the thread returns to the spider, so all things return to the Imperishable, and the returning is not an ending but a gathering home.
2: The shining, higher than heaven, than which nothing is subtler, than which nothing is greater — that is the Self, the Purusha, within the heart. He is seen in the cave of the heart by the pure in heart, and the seeing is the finding, and the finding is the peace.

Take as your bow the great weapon of the Upanishad; place upon it the arrow sharpened by meditation. Draw it with a mind absorbed in Him, and strike, O gentle one — the mark, the Imperishable. Om is the bow, the soul is the arrow, and Brahman is the target. It is to be struck by an unwavering mind; and he who strikes it becomes one with the target, like the arrow.

He who knows that highest home of Brahman, wherein all the worlds are established and shine — he, the knower of Brahman, becomes Brahman. He crosses beyond sorrow; he crosses beyond sin; freed from the knots of the heart, he becomes immortal. The wise who know him in the space within the heart are freed from this world — they are the great ones, and their going forth is not a leaving but an arriving.
3: Two birds, inseparable companions, cling to the same tree. One of them eats the sweet fruit; the other looks on without eating. On the same tree, the person is sunk in sorrow, bewildered by his own helplessness. But when he sees the other, the Lord, worshipful and great, his sorrow passes away — and the passing is the whole of the teaching.

Truth alone triumphs, not falsehood. By truth the path to the gods is spread — the path the sages travel, the desireless, to the highest treasure of truth. Truth alone triumphs — and this is the teaching carved on the pillar of the lion, and the pillar stands, and the teaching outlasts every empire that ignored it.

Wide-spread in the front, wide-spread in the rear, wide-spread in the south and the north — Brahman alone is all this, the highest, the best. Having known this, the wise become immortal — for immortality is not a length of days but a largeness of being, and the largeness is already yours, and the knowing is the claiming.
